clue.text: Old Testament prophet seen in tam-o'-shanter

indicators.note: the answer can be seen sitting inside the next words

parts.note: the letters run from the second letter of 'tam' to the first of 'shanter', skipping the hyphens and apostrophe

explanation.surface: A biblical prophet spotted wearing a Scottish bonnet.
explanation.walkthrough: Punctuation inside the fodder is ignored. A tam-o'-shanter is a flat woollen Scottish cap with a bobble.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain definition by category: the named figure has his own short book among the minor prophets.

clue.text: Historic ship showing might on river

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece sits on top of the other

parts.note: might and may are both verbs of possibility
a river is something that flows: a flow-er

explanation.surface: A famous old vessel displaying its power out on the water.
explanation.walkthrough: "River" as a thing that flows is a classic crossword trick. The noun 'might' is really the verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: the ship that carried the Pilgrims from England to America in 1620 is famous in history.

clue.text: Quiet location for milk … shake

parts.note: the call for silence
where a cow's milk is held

explanation.surface: A peaceful spot for dairy, trailing off into a milkshake.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis makes you read 'milk … shake' as one drink, but 'shake' stands apart as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain verb synonym: both mean to tremble violently, as with fear or cold.

clue.text: Intensity regularly dropped in avian protection

indicators.note: every other letter is dropped, at regular intervals

parts.note: drop the odd letters I, T, N, I, Y and keep the even ones

explanation.surface: Some force has been lost from a bird's defences.
explanation.walkthrough: Which set goes, odds or evens, is for the solver to test; here the first letter goes.
explanation.definitionFit: A fresh description rather than a synonym: the structure birds build shelters their eggs and chicks.

clue.text: Annoys the French (a primary requirement)?

parts.note: a basic requirement is a need
French plural 'the'

explanation.surface: A put-upon Brit grumbling that the French always come first.
explanation.walkthrough: The brackets and question mark hint that the bracketed requirement comes first, ahead of the French word, though it is printed second. 'The French' could be LE or LA; only the plural fits.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain verb synonym: to needle someone is to provoke or irritate them with small jabs.

clue.text: Energy shown by Second XI?

parts.note: the standard abbreviation
eleven players make a football or cricket team

explanation.surface: The reserve side showing plenty of vigour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second XI' reads as the reserve team, but it splits into an abbreviation plus a side of eleven.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiomatic sense, as in running out of steam or picking up steam.

clue.text: Pinches small tissues

parts.note: the clothing-size abbreviation
disposable cleaning cloths

explanation.surface: Someone nicking little packs of tissues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pinches' means steals here, not squeezes.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal synonyms: both are casual British slang for stealing.

clue.text: Shaking tail end, watch a lad fall in Vermont, for example?

indicators.note: to shake off is to get rid of, so the first word loses its last letter

parts.note: to watch is to see
the verb loses its final E
as printed
a boy, someone's son

explanation.surface: Someone warns a boy wagging about near the edge not to tumble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fall' looks like a tumble, but it is the American word for autumn; New England states like Vermont are famous for fall foliage, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example with a regional word: fall is the American name for autumn, one of the four.

clue.text: 'How eerie!' 'Why, sure!' Uneasy sentiment when abroad

indicators.note: letters that are not at ease get shuffled around

parts.note: the fifteen letters of HOW EERIE WHY SURE rearranged

explanation.surface: Two nervous exclamations from someone unsettled while travelling overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: The quote marks dress the fodder up as dialogue; ignore them and count the fifteen letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A fresh description of a stock phrase: it is the classic line scrawled on a holiday postcard home.

clue.text: TikTok etc, therefore claim idea is deranged

indicators.note: the letters go out of their proper order

parts.note: as in 'so it follows'
CLAIM IDEA rearranged

explanation.surface: A grumble that online platforms breed crazy notions.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a verdict on TikTok, but 'therefore' just supplies two letters up front.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: TikTok is one platform of the class, and 'etc' widens it to the whole category.

clue.text: On the phone, Ms Raducanu will call Ireland

indicators.note: you only hear the words, so it is their sound that counts

parts.note: Emma Raducanu, British tennis player; will = 'LL; call = DIAL

explanation.surface: Tennis star Emma Raducanu is going to ring Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: Emma Raducanu won the 2021 US Open. Said quickly in a non-rhotic British accent, the three words run together into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A poetic nickname: the country is called this for its green landscape.

clue.text: Chose, after imbibing drop of Laphroaig, to become drunk

indicators.note: the first word drinks the next piece in

parts.note: to choose is to pick

indicators.note: just a drop, the first letter

parts.note: first letter of Laphroaig

explanation.surface: Someone picks a whisky and sips it until tipsy.
explanation.walkthrough: Laphroaig is a peaty Islay single malt whisky, so 'drop' suits the surface while meaning just one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal slang: being preserved in alcohol is a jokey way of saying intoxicated.

clue.text: Moves heavily wanting sleep after cycling

indicators.note: the letters go round like a wheel, so the first moves to the end

parts.note: slumber is sleep; everything after its first letter stays in place
the leading S of slumber cycles round to the back

explanation.surface: A tired rider trudges along craving a nap after a bike ride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycling' suggests a bike ride but asks for the letters to rotate.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain verb synonym: to move in a slow, clumsy, weighty way.

clue.text: With buff back muscles, doing a flip, they're resolute

indicators.note: flip the letters end to end

parts.note: buff and straw are both pale yellow colours
latissimus dorsi, the broad back muscles

explanation.surface: Gym-goers with ripped backs do somersaults, full of determination.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buff' reads as muscular, which fits the gym picture, but here it is the colour. The whole string is read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: stalwarts are loyal, steadfast supporters, people who hold firm.

clue.text: Tax channel

definitions.meaning: a verb: to tax or exhaust someone's energy
a noun: a conduit that carries water away

explanation.surface: A heading about money routed to the revenue.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words look like nouns about finance or TV, but 'tax' is the verb meaning to strain.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: the verb meaning to sap or exhaust, and the noun for a pipe or gutter carrying liquid away.

clue.text: Using reason, conciliated freely? That's not on!

indicators.note: the letters move freely into a new order
read literally: that is without ON

parts.note: the fodder with O and N taken out

explanation.surface: Someone objects to a peace deal reached too loosely by argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's not on!' sounds like an outraged exclamation, but it tells you to take ON out of the fodder before shuffling.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjectival sense: dialectic reasoning proceeds by argument and counter-argument.

clue.text: Wristwatch, say: not so exciting but a becoming one

indicators.note: the letter A turns into I, the Roman numeral one

parts.note: tamer means less wild

explanation.surface: A wristwatch is dull, yet somehow flattering to wear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Becoming' tempts you to read 'attractive', but it means turning into.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a wristwatch is one kind of device that keeps time, flagged by 'say'.

clue.text: Turncoats abandoning HMS inhabited this island, primarily?

definitions.text: Turncoats abandoning HMS inhabited this island, primarily?

indicators.note: take the first, or primary, letter of each word

parts.words: Turncoats abandoning HMS inhabited this island
parts.note: the initial of each of the six words

explanation.surface: The Bounty mutineers left their ship and settled on this island.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too. The italicised HMS hints at a ship's name left unsaid: the Bounty.
explanation.definitionFit: An &lit: after the 1789 mutiny on HMS Bounty, the mutineers (turncoats) did settle on this Pacific island.

clue.text: Like a competition involving multiple setters?

definitions.text: Like a competition involving multiple setters?

parts.note: surface: any contest; meant: a ruthless one where rivals tear each other apart
surface: several crossword compilers; meant: setter dogs, one breed pitted against another

explanation.surface: A contest between several crossword compilers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setters' suggests crossword setters, but the clue means the gun-dog breed, so the contest is canine against canine.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: a ruthlessly competitive situation is described with this hyphenated phrase.

clue.text: Scribble, leave hurriedly

definitions.meaning: to write a note quickly and carelessly

explanation.surface: Jot a note and rush out.
explanation.walkthrough: The two halves read as one hurried action; each is a separate meaning of the same phrasal verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses of one phrasal verb: writing something rapidly, and departing at speed.

clue.text: Understand second Beatles hit

parts.note: to get it is to understand
to second a motion is to support it

explanation.surface: Grasping the Beatles' follow-up single.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second' looks like an ordinal, as in their second hit, but it is the verb meaning support.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the song was a 1969 number one for the band.

clue.text: They're beyond help? King George succeeded in the protection of one

indicators.note: the outer letters shelter the inner piece

parts.note: Georgius Rex, George the King
the abbreviation used in family trees
as printed

explanation.surface: A monarch took over while guarding someone past saving.
explanation.walkthrough: The king's cipher and the S together form the shelter; 'one' slips in after the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal noun: a goner is someone doomed or past saving, and the question mark flags the loose phrasing.

clue.text: Ghastly duck penetrating — we need camouflage!

indicators.note: the piece pushes its way into the others

parts.note: to camouflage is to hide
a duck is zero in cricket, shaped like O
we becomes us

explanation.surface: Panic as a horrible duck breaks through: we need to take cover!
explanation.walkthrough: The outer pieces are read in reverse clue order, camouflage first, with the duck wedged between.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain adjective synonym: both mean horribly ugly or shocking.

clue.text: Where to get dates and a drink for '90s rockers

definitions.text: Where to get dates and a drink
definitions.meaning: a desert spring where date palms grow
the Manchester band fronted by the Gallagher brothers

explanation.surface: A venue for a date and a drink with an ageing rock crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dates' suggests romance, but they are the fruit that grows by desert water. The band was a leading 1990s Britpop act.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a fertile desert spot with water and date palms, and the band that dominated 1990s British rock.

clue.text: Erstwhile capital offence: agent provocateur finally taken, 7 beheaded

indicators.note: take the last letter of each word
a beheaded word has lost its head, so its first letter goes

parts.note: last letters of agenT provocateuR
the answer to 7 down, minus its first letter

explanation.surface: A spy who stirred up trouble has at last been caught and executed.
explanation.walkthrough: '7' points to the answer of 7 down. In the UK this crime carried the death penalty until 1998, hence 'erstwhile'.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: betraying one's country was once punishable by death in Britain.

clue.text: Liberally salt the roast, say? Who does that any more?

indicators.note: the letters are treated freely, not kept in order

parts.note: the fifteen letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone sneers at heavily seasoning the Sunday joint as old-fashioned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like the usual signal for an example, but its letters are part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiomatic equivalents: both are scornful ways of dismissing something as out of fashion.

clue.text: Everyman gripped by American science fiction? Hardly

parts.note: the standard abbreviation

indicators.note: the piece is held inside the next one

parts.note: the genre's abbreviation
the setter speaking of himself

explanation.surface: The setter caught up in a US sci-fi story, which seems unlikely.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter's name in the clue usually stands for I or ME.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal interjection: both scornfully dismiss something as very unlikely.

clue.text: What pothead may get from — or do to — his habit

explanation.surface: A cannabis user's relationship with the drug.
explanation.walkthrough: The dashes set up one shared 'his habit' for both halves: the buzz you get from it and what you do when you quit.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a thrill or buzz, and the verb in the idiom for giving up an addiction.
